source: Wikipedia articles that record a specific event on one atlas island, with an open-licence photograph of the subject

rows.title: A wave over the lantern
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1985, the lighthouse was struck by a rogue wave about 48 metres (157 feet) high.
rows.summary: In 1985 a rogue wave about 48 metres high struck the lighthouse on Fastnet Rock. The light stands on the most southerly point of Ireland, south-west of Cape Clear. The tower that took the wave is the second built on the rock.

rows.title: The little cave's scar
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1945, a mine exploded near Boat Cave, causing damage to the cliff face, which is still visible.
rows.summary: In 1945 a mine exploded in the sea beside Boat Cave, on the south-west shore of Staffa. The blast damaged the cliff, and the scar is still visible. Boat Cave is the small opening beside Mackinnon's Cave, not the great arch of Fingal's Cave.
rows.image_note: Boat Cave, the small cave on the south-west of Staffa
rows.image_alt: Boat Cave, the small cave on the south-west of Staffa

rows.title: Torched on the tide
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: A small garrison was stationed in the castle until the Jacobite rising of 1715 when Allan recaptured and torched it, purportedly to keep it out of the hands of Hanoverian forces.
rows.summary: Castle Tioram stands on the tidal island of Eilean Tioram, in Loch Moidart. During the Jacobite rising of 1715, Allan of Clanranald took the castle back and burned it, so Hanoverian forces would not hold it. The tower has been empty since that fire.

rows.title: Fire on the rock light
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1968, a third lighthouse was built on the Calf after a severe fire destroyed the Chicken Rock light.
rows.summary: In 1968 a severe fire destroyed the light on Chicken Rock, the islet south-west of the Calf of Man. A replacement light was built on the Calf because of that fire. The tower on Chicken Rock was later rebuilt.

rows.title: The last two families
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The island was inhabited until 1855, when the Lord Proprietor Augustus Smith removed the remaining population from the island.
rows.summary: Samson was inhabited until 1855, when Augustus Smith, Lord Proprietor of Scilly, removed the last two families. They had been living mainly on limpets and potatoes. He then made a deer park, and the deer escaped the walls.
rows.image_note: Samson, in the Isles of Scilly
rows.image_alt: Samson, in the Isles of Scilly

rows.title: The tow parted
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: There is one identified shipwreck, a steamship named The Pioneer, which ran ashore in 1878 with a cargo of iron bars when the tow lines to it broke following its rescue from engine failure near the Skerries.
rows.summary: In 1878 the steamship Pioneer ran ashore on Puffin Island, off eastern Anglesey, carrying iron bars. She had already lost her engines near the Skerries and was being towed when the tow lines broke. The island's record names this as its one identified wreck.

rows.title: The winter on the island
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Like Lilburne, he never regained his liberty, dying on Drake's Island in the winter of 1683.
rows.summary: John Lambert, a general in the New Model Army, was brought to Drake's Island from Guernsey, where he had been a prisoner since 1662. He was never freed. He died on the island in the winter of 1683.

rows.title: The relics were divided
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The series of Viking raids on Iona began in 794 and, after its treasures had been plundered many times, Columba's relics were removed and divided two ways between Scotland and Ireland in 849 as the monastery was abandoned.
rows.summary: Viking raids on Iona began in 794. In 849, after the monastery had been plundered again and again, Columba's relics were removed and split between Scotland and Ireland. The community then left the island.

rows.title: Outside the excise
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: They claimed that the island was outside the jurisdiction of the excise men until a court case in 1884.
rows.summary: The inn on Steep Holm sold rum and tobacco bought from passing ships. Its keepers said the island stood outside the excise. A court case in 1884 rejected that claim.

rows.title: Seven years on the rock
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: in 1744 ... transportation to the Mewstone, where he was interned for seven years.
rows.summary: In 1744 Sam Wakeman was interned on the Great Mew Stone, off Wembury, for seven years, rather than being transported. He stayed after the term and paid rent in rabbits for the manor. He is credited with cutting the rough stone steps to the summit.
rows.image_note: The Great Mew Stone, off Wembury
rows.image_alt: The Great Mew Stone, off Wembury

rows.title: The cradle taken down
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1864, the laird's factor, Mr Walker, had the cradle dismantled on the grounds of safety, and had a wall erected on the neighbouring cliff on Noss.
rows.summary: For about two centuries a cradle ran across the gap from Noss to the Holm of Noss, large enough for one man and a sheep. In 1864 the factor, Mr Walker, had the hoist dismantled because it was unsafe. A wall was built on the Noss cliff in its place.

rows.image_alt: The Holm of Noss, across the gap from Noss

rows.title: After the fire at Sandaig
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: He moved here after his home at Sandaig, which he called Camusfeàrna in his books, was destroyed by fire in 1968.
rows.summary: In 1968 fire destroyed Gavin Maxwell's house at Sandaig. He moved to Eilean Bàn, between Kyle of Lochalsh and Skye, and planned a zoo and a book on British wild animals there. Both were given up when he died in 1969.

rows.title: The correspondent's ship
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: A pub was opened in 2003, named Byron Darnton after the vessel which wrecked on the island in 1946.
rows.summary: In 1946 the ship Byron Darnton was wrecked on Sanda, the island off the Mull of Kintyre. She was named for an American war correspondent. A pub opened on the island in 2003 took the ship's name.

rows.title: Hidden after Pinkie
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1547 the priory served as a refuge for Mary, Queen of Scots, aged four, hidden here for a few weeks following the disastrous defeat of the Scots army at the Battle of Pinkie Cleugh during the Rough Wooing.
rows.summary: In 1547, after the defeat at Pinkie Cleugh, Mary, Queen of Scots, then aged four, was hidden for a few weeks in the priory on Inchmahome. The island lies in the Lake of Menteith. The English were pressing Stirling, and the lake was the refuge.
